_comment: URLs a block attribute can carry, and what each side has to make of them. Read by tests/js/validation.test.js and tests/php/Paypal_Payment_Buttons_Test.php, so a rebuild that lands on one side only fails a test on the other. `accepted` and `rejected` are where the two agree: the same output from both, or nothing from either. `strictEditor` and `parserSplit` are where they differ, and both pin BOTH outputs, so closing a gap fails as loudly as opening one. `strictEditor` is a decision — the canvas injects a script src into wp-admin, so it takes https alone, where the published page would rather repair the scheme than drop a button a merchant already has. `parserSplit` is an accident the two live with: `new URL()` and `wp_parse_url()` reading the same bytes differently. A `why` is prose for whoever reads the row next, and carries no assertion. What each parser makes of a URL it has already accepted — whitespace, tabs, control characters, `%2e`, which characters it percent-encodes — is left unpinned: that set is unbounded, safe on both sides, and pinning it would fail the suite on a PHP or browser bump for nothing. The host list is pinned by test_paypal_host_allow_lists_are_in_sync() instead.

accepted.name: the SDK URL a stacked payment reads back
a sandbox SDK URL from PayPal's stacked button snippet
a payment link
a payment link already carrying the BN code
the sandbox host
paypal.com without the www
sandbox.paypal.com without the www
no query string
an empty query string
accepted.why: URL.search is '' for a bare `?`, and the PHP drops an empty query rather than rebuilding one. It has to: PHP 8.0 began reporting `query => ''` where 7.4 left the key out, so keeping it would put a `?` on the end on one PHP and not the other. Same resource either way.

accepted.name: a path off the SDK route
a deep path
the default port spelled out
a port that is not the default
a fully qualified host
a fully qualified sandbox host
a host in mixed case
a fragment, which neither side keeps
credentials on a PayPal host, which neither side keeps
PayPal's copy-html snippet, with the separators HTML-escaped
escaped and raw separators in one query
every component at once
an escaped separator in the path, which is not a separator
an entity in upper case, which is not one
a percent-encoded ampersand in a value, which stays encoded
a percent-encoded entity in a value, which stays encoded

rejected.name: the host from the security report
a host that only starts the same
a subdomain of a PayPal host
a PayPal host used as userinfo
a PayPal host used as a password
a javascript: URL wearing a PayPal host
rejected.why: The string the allow-list was written for: it parses with a PayPal hostname on both sides, so only the scheme tells it from a real SDK URL. The rebuild onto https kept it harmless before either side checked the scheme; both check it now.

rejected.name: an ftp: URL on a PayPal host
rejected.why: Same shape as the row above, with a scheme that is merely wrong rather than dangerous. It holds each side's scheme check to what it accepts: http and https on the published page, https alone on the canvas.

rejected.name: a wss: URL on a PayPal host
rejected.why: A scheme `new URL()` treats as special, so the hostname parses out of it the same way. A script src or an href still has to refuse it.

strictEditor.name: plain HTTP
strictEditor.why: The canvas injects this as a script src inside wp-admin, so it takes https alone. The published page repairs the scheme instead of dropping a button a merchant already has: a block attribute is hand-editable JSON in the comment delimiter and survives an import, and the rebuild lands on https either way.

parserSplit.name: a scheme-relative URL
parserSplit.why: wp_parse_url() reads an authority off the leading //, and the absent scheme is repaired to https like plain HTTP above. `new URL()` with no base throws on the same bytes, so the canvas stops there.

parserSplit.name: an authority PayPal only appears to own
parserSplit.why: `new URL()` fills in the missing slashes and walks the dot segments; wp_parse_url() finds only a path, `www.paypal.com/../../wp-content/uploads/x.txt`, and no host. Both outcomes are safe — this is the string the rebuild exists for — but the canvas previews a URL the published page drops.

parserSplit.name: a backslash where the path should start
parserSplit.why: `new URL()` reads a backslash as a path separator, so the authority ends at paypal.com and evil.test becomes a path segment. wp_parse_url() keeps the whole of `www.paypal.com\evil.test` as the host, which then misses the allow-list. Same class as the row above, and the same reason the canvas rebuilds rather than passing the string through.

parserSplit.name: ideographic full stops in the host
parserSplit.why: `new URL()` runs IDNA, which maps U+3002 to a label separator, so the host allow-list sees www.paypal.com. parse_url() runs none, and the host misses the list whatever the build makes of the bytes — some, macOS among them, replace the U+3002 continuation bytes with `_` first, since parse_url() strips whatever the local iscntrl() calls a control character. Both safe; the canvas is the more permissive one, and what it returns is a genuine PayPal URL.

parserSplit.name: no path at all
parserSplit.why: `new URL()` always hands back a pathname; the PHP appends a path only when parse_url() reports one. Same resource either way.
